w: Dr. Kaur taught this session in class on Oct 29 (the class capture) with her updated slide deck. Her question for the session: are dental implants contraindicated in periodontally compromised patients? Her answer at the end: no, not once the periodontitis is treated, arrested and the patient is compliant. On the way there she built the picture of peri-implant health and disease the same way you already picture periodontal health, gingivitis and periodontitis. Success versus survival "Be cautious of the terms used, success versus survival." A surviving implant is simply present in the mouth and restored, in other words loaded. A surviving implant can still have biologic complications (peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, bone loss, inflammation) and prosthetic complications (a fractured abutment, a loose screw, a fractured crown, even a fractured implant), or simply pain or mucosal recession. A successful implant is restored and free of any complication, clinically and radiographically. When you read implant studies, check which one they measured. The success criteria on the slide are Albrektsson's, from 1986: the implant is immobile; there is no peri-implant radiolucency; there is no pain, infection, paresthesia or neuropathy; and after 1 year in function, vertical bone loss is 1.5 mm or less. In class she added the rest of the criterion: after that first year, no more than 0.2 mm of vertical bone loss a year. A radiolucency at the apical third of an implant is called retrograde peri-implantitis. The 2017 classification: peri-implant health and disease From 1986 to 2017 there was no agreed classification of health and disease around implants. The 2017 World Workshop added one alongside the new periodontal classification: peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, and peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiencies. Peri-implant health. No clinical signs of inflammation (no change in color, no edema, no redness); no bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; no increase in probing depth compared with previous examinations; and no bone loss beyond the crestal bone level changes from initial remodeling. Notice there is no 3 mm cutoff. A healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm: the tissue height around it depends on how deep the implant was placed, the height of the abutment, and the tissue itself (a narrow implant in a wide ridge leaves extra tissue). Probing an implant is also hard to do accurately, even with a plastic probe. So every measurement is compared with that implant's own baseline: capture the clinical and radiographic baseline, or you will have nothing to compare to going forward. Crestal remodeling. Once an implant is put in function, the crestal bone adapts to the new load. In class she put a number on it, which the slide doesn't: about 2 mm of remodeling, which plateaus within about the first year. That is physiologic. Any bone loss beyond it is pathologic. Peri-implant mucositis, the implant's version of gingivitis. Signs of inflammation; profuse (line or drop) bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; an increase in probing depth compared with baseline; and no bone loss beyond initial remodeling. The deeper pocket comes from inflamed, swollen tissue, not from bone loss. Like gingivitis it is reversible, so take it seriously: don't just put it on watch. A probing depth can only grow for three reasons: an inaccurate measurement, inflammation adding volume to the tissue, or true bone loss. Suppuration (pus) is a sign of active disease, around a tooth or an implant, and it always needs a response now, whatever the long-term plan: local debridement, and sometimes a local antibiotic at a deep site (Dr. Litz covers antibiotics in Session 8). Peri-implantitis. Signs of inflammation; bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; increased probing depth compared with previous exams; and bone loss beyond the crestal changes from initial remodeling. "When somebody talks about peri-implantitis, you should have a picture of true bone loss in your mind." The definition on the slide: a plaque-associated pathological condition in the tissues around implants, characterized by inflammation in the peri-implant mucosa and subsequent progressive loss of supporting bone. The definition itself says the disease runs from inflammation to bone loss, which is why it must be controlled at the mucositis stage. Why is it so hard to treat? Rebuilding bone around an implant should be easier than true periodontal regeneration: there is no PDL or cementum to regrow, only bone fill, so only osteoblasts are needed. The problem is the surface. Implants are made rough (acid-etched, blasted), even nano-rough, because osteoblasts love it, and so does plaque. No product is better than another at decontaminating the implant surface: saline, chlorhexidine (Peridex), citric acid, EDTA and lasers give the same or similar results. Bone loss around implants also tends not to form the deep, narrow, vertical defects that regenerate best, and disease recurs often. Still, a case with a deep buccal pocket (8-9 mm), suppuration, bleeding and bone loss, but with the mesial and distal bone peaks and the lingual plate intact, is still worth treating: open it, clean it, place a biologic and/or bone graft, cover it with a barrier membrane and close. Peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiency is loss of the mucosa along with the bone under it. Often bone is lost while the mucosal margin stays put; with a long-standing disease or risk factors such as a thin phenotype, which recedes faster than a thick one, the tissue goes too. Ailing, failing, failed (Meffert 1992) This classification describes the implant's state and tells you what to do. An ailing implant has static radiographic bone loss with no inflammation and no mobility: the loss stopped, on its own or because someone intervened. Monitor it, and capture the clinical and radiographic data at each visit. A failing implant has progressive bone loss and signs of inflammation, but no mobility: it is still in function, and what you do varies case by case (for example, keep an 89-year-old's implants at #18 and #19 when taking them out would leave too little bone above the inferior alveolar nerve to rebuild). A failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function. Unlike a tooth, a mobile implant has only one treatment: remove it. Mobility of the implant body means loss of osseointegration, which "nobody in this universe can reverse." First confirm the mobility is in the implant body, not the abutment or the crown. Loss of osseointegration is usually not from peri-implantitis: implants rarely become mobile from peri-implantitis, even with only a third of the implant left in bone. An implant with bone loss that advanced is still judged failed, mobile or not, when it has no future. Etiology, microbiology and risk factors Peri-implant disease is multifactorial, but "if somebody has to ask you" how it starts, the answer is bacteria: plaque biofilm. Periodontitis and peri-implantitis share causative bacteria. The slide groups the risk factors as patient-related, surgical/implant-related, soft tissue and prosthetic. Risk factors for peri-implant mucositis (slide): smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, thin soft tissue phenotype, and obesity and/or metabolic syndrome. Risk factors for peri-implantitis: smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, obesity and/or metabolic syndrome, implant malposition, uncontrolled diabetes, limited bone width, and depression or antidepressant medications. Poor plaque control carried an odds ratio of 14.3 (Ferreira et al. 2006). Other factors on the slide: systemic disease, lack of keratinized tissue and parafunctional habits. Microbiology. The flora of the mouth before implantation determines the flora around the implant. The flora around stable implants resembles the subgingival flora of a healthy dentate patient. The etiology of peri-implantitis is probably multifactorial, and genetic factors play an important role. The pellicle starts forming on the implant as early as 30 minutes after it is exposed in the mouth. The early colonizers are mostly gram-positive cocci and rods, including Actinomyces, just as on teeth; as the biofilm matures, the periodontal pathogens (P. gingivalis, P. intermedia and others), gram-negative anaerobes, cause both peri-implantitis and periodontitis. Why the patient lost their teeth matters Yes, it matters. A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host, and susceptibility to periodontal disease raises the risk of peri-implant disease, even in a fully edentulous mouth. Putative periodontal pathogens may persist even a year after periodontally involved teeth are extracted. Definitive treatment of periodontitis is critical to success, and untreated periodontitis is a contraindication to implant therapy. A patient whose periodontitis has been treated and is in maintenance can receive implants like anyone else, with a maintenance plan matched to their risk. The order matters. For a patient with advanced bone loss and heavy calculus: scaling and root planing first; extract the hopeless teeth in the disease-control phase without immediate implants; let everything heal with good oral hygiene instructions; re-evaluate after Phase I; do any Phase II pocket elimination surgery; and only then plan implants, once pockets are reduced and the patient's hygiene has changed. Risk assessment happens again at placement, at the prosthetic phase and at every maintenance visit. Two-stage and single-stage. In a two-stage implant, a cover screw closes the implant and the tissue is closed over it to heal. About 3-4 months later it is uncovered, a healing abutment (transmucosal: it comes through the mucosa) is attached, and after about 2-3 weeks the impression is made with a prosthetic abutment. In a single-stage implant the healing abutment goes on at placement, when bone and tissue are ideal, saving a second surgery. The #31 case. A 41-year-old man with untreated periodontitis had implant #31 placed, with bone graft at the distal of #30, and then no follow-up or maintenance. The graft could not regenerate between avascular cementum and metal in a diseased mouth. Two years after placement he came back with food packing, his only complaint, and loss of hard and soft tissue around #31 (a peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiency). The implant was removed with a reverse-torque tool. One option was a root canal and resection of #30's distal root, then grafting and a new #31 implant; the case was instead treated more aggressively: #30 was extracted with socket conversion, the ridge was rebuilt vertically, and implants were placed at #30 and #31. Extracting #30 gave the graft a high bone peak on the mesial to grow against. The European Association for Osseointegration's 2006 Zurich consensus found significantly more peri-implantitis and marginal bone loss in people who lost teeth to periodontitis. In the study she showed (Roccuzzo 2010, 10 years) healthy, moderately and severely compromised patients were compared on survival alone, and the compromised groups lost more implants; complications would be higher still. Supportive peri-implant therapy (SPIT) follows the 2024 AO/AAP consensus. Challenges of periodontally compromised patients Periodontally compromised teeth have attachment loss, pockets, alveolar bone loss and tooth loss. For implants that means: Soft tissue loss: papillary loss, black triangles and loss of keratinized tissue, more pronounced on the thin periodontium phenotype. Recession loses keratinized gingiva first, and the tissue's thickness changes too; both the amount of keratinized tissue and its thickness guide the implant's health. This matters most in the esthetic zone, where loss of hard and soft tissue can also come from trauma. Reduced bone volume: biomechanical concerns, and implant fractures from an unfavorable crown-implant ratio. Bone width is far easier to grow than height. A sinus lift is relatively easy height, because the bone grows into the sinus, not into the mouth. In one case (missing #1-7, implants at #2, 3, 4 and 6) the vertical defect was too great: the anterior implants were lost and the patient, who wanted something fixed, ended up with a removable implant-supported prosthesis. Bone grafting options (slide): socket conversion, ridge augmentation and sinus lifts; nerve repositioning or short implants; and distraction osteogenesis for vertical augmentation. Risk assessment and risk factors Risk assessment is done before implant placement, during the osseointegration period, during implant maintenance, and after the removal of an implant: at every stage, not once. Any risk factor that increases the risk of periodontitis also increases the risk of implant failure, and untreated or partially treated periodontal disease leads more often to implant failure. Smoking works on three fronts. Microbiology: smokers harbor different, more virulent plaque bacteria, and A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis and B. forsythus are harder to eradicate in current smokers; smoking depletes oxygen, and the gram-negative anaerobes love that. Immunology: impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, fewer T helper cells and B lymphocytes, more IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and more collagenase activity. Physiology: nicotine impairs revascularization in soft and hard tissue, the first step of healing after surgery. The numbers: Bain and Moy 1993, 2,194 implants, failure rate 11.3% in smokers vs 4.76% in nonsmokers; Alsaadi 2007, a dose-response relationship, with worse rates in heavy smokers; Simonis 2010, peri-implantitis in 23.53% of smokers vs 16.51% of nonsmokers. Dose-response means the higher the dose, the worse the outcome: years of smoking and cigarettes a day both count, and risk starts below a pack (20) a day. Vaping: little long-term evidence; there is no combustion, so the vasoconstrictive effect on healing may be missing, but the immune response is still suppressed. Diabetes. The duration of diabetes did not affect implant survival under optimal glycemic control. A periodontally healthy environment is essential along with good glycemic levels, and implant therapy is contraindicated with poorly controlled diabetes. The measure is glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), the gold standard, because it reflects the last 3-4 months, the lifespan of red blood cells. Get the lab value for your records. (Not part of the lecture, she added: UAB's clinic uses an HbA1c of 8 or higher as a contraindication, and a patient's value can come down, so keep reassessing.) From the class exam-review guide (not in this year's slides): IL-1 gene polymorphisms are linked to a hyper-responsive inflammatory reaction to bacteria, and a positive IL-1 genotype plus smoking has a synergistic effect, the highest peri-implantitis risk. In class she listed genetic traits and a family history of periodontitis among the risk factors to weigh. Maintenance: probing, bleeding and radiographs Implants are maintained with implant probes (plastic) and implant scalers, different from the SRP instruments; many healthy implants need little cleaning. The diagnostic criteria for peri-implant evaluation (Lang and Berglundh 2011): bleeding on probing (with a light force, about 0.25 N), soft tissue evaluation, suppuration, probing depth, pain or tenderness, mobility and radiographic bone loss. Bleeding on probing depends on the tissue's condition and on the probing force. It can be caused by an inappropriate probing force or angulation, or by inflammation of the marginal tissue. Its absence is a good predictor of stable peri-implant conditions; its presence indicates inflammation but may not predict progression. Look at the type of bleeding: a little blood that appears slowly may not mean disease, but profuse bleeding that fills the sulcus as you probe does. Track it over visits. In the study on the slide, sites that bled at 4 of 4 visits had a 30% chance of attachment loss; 3 of 4, 14%; 2 of 4, 6%; 1 of 4, 3%; and sites with no bleeding at any of 4 visits, 1.5%. Bleeding on probing is a limited but useful prognostic indicator. Radiographs are taken at: implant placement; before the Phase II uncovery surgery (or before the prosthetic phase if one-stage); the final impression; final abutment seating; the final cementation or restoration (the baseline radiograph); every 6 months for the first year; and annually after that. Extra radiographs are indicated at a maintenance visit when the clinical signs point to disease: increased probing depth, bleeding on probing, suppuration. "Radiographs are confirmatory rather than exploratory" (Lang and Hill 1977): read them together with the clinical findings. Conclusions Risk assessment and control of risk factors are an integral part of implant therapy. Discuss the increased risk of peri-implantitis with a patient who has a history of periodontal disease or other risk factors. Treat any periodontal infection before starting implant therapy. Compliance with plaque control and regular maintenance decides the result, and much of it is in the patient's hands: make them your co-therapist. A treated, arrested, compliant patient with a history of periodontitis is not a contraindication for implants.
